case.label: D
case.text: A reader who sees 'several hours' and 'keep retrying' may pick the retry-policy change as the least-effort fix, since SNS already retries HTTPS deliveries and a longer policy looks like it keeps the event without a new queue. It fails because the total retry time of an HTTP/S delivery policy is capped at 3,600 seconds (checked in the saved SNS retries page), so 24 hours is not a valid setting, and a retry policy never hands the event back to the company for resending. Option C is the next-strongest distractor: it is plausible only if the reader forgets that an SNS dead-letter queue attaches to a subscription, not to a topic. Option A would also store failed events but has far more operational overhead than a dead-letter queue. Weak points of the item: B and E are interdependent (E is the prerequisite of B, and B alone has no queue policy), so a reader may doubt whether E counts as an 'action that meets the requirement'; and the pair B and E is also the only two options that name an SQS standard queue, which is a mild wording cue.

case.label: C
case.text: A polling Lambda function that compares DescribeInstances output every minute would detect every stop within a few minutes, from any cause (console, script or schedule), and could send the email and create the ticket, so it technically meets the functional requirement. It loses only on the explicit LEAST operational overhead criterion (custom code, state to compare, IAM permissions, scaling with the fleet), which the stem states clearly. Option A is wrong on substance (StatusCheckFailed is not a stop event); option D is wrong on substance and wiring (CloudTrail logs to S3 do not notify). The stem names the three stop paths, which cues an event-based answer, and the stem does not say the Lambda function accepts an EventBridge event, but the existing function as a target is the normal pattern, so no constraint is missing.

answers.flag: Option D (delete each successfully processed message, then return an error) also leaves only the malformed message to be retried, so a careful candidate could defend it; only the phrase 'MOST operationally efficient' (extra SQS API calls and permissions in code versus a mapping setting) separates A from D.

case.label: D
case.text: Deleting each message that succeeds from inside the function and then failing the invocation is a long-documented workaround for partial batch failure: after the error, only the undeleted malformed message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout, and it moves to the dead-letter queue after the receive count is exhausted. That does 'retry only the malformed message' without any event source mapping setting. It costs more code, needs sqs:DeleteMessage permission and the queue URL, and adds a failure mode (a delete can fail), which is why A is more operationally efficient, but the stem's wording leaves D defensible on the functional requirement. Option B does not stop good messages from being retried; option C sends failure records to another queue and does not retry only the bad message, and an on-failure destination is not the SQS mechanism for this problem.
